turns.question: What are the three parts of a user story?
turns.text:
A user story has three parts, named by Ron Jeffries: the card, the conversation, and the confirmation.

- **Card:** "one or two sentences, traditionally handwritten on an index card, used for planning and as a reminder." [S2]
- **Conversation:** "the discussions between customer and developers where the details get worked out." [S2]
- **Confirmation:** "the tests that capture those details and show when the story is done." [S3]

The card is the least important of the three. [S1] The source also says that stories are not contracts: the tests, not the card, are the record of what was agreed. [S3]

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Each chapter section has the same shape: a one-line summary, the main ideas, and a takeaway. A glossary and two quick-reference tables are at the end. The book in one page If you only remember ten things from the book, these are the ones to keep. Requirements are a communication problem. The people who want software and the people who build it see the world differently. A method works when neither side dominates and both share the trade-off between scope and time. A story has three parts: a short written reminder (the card), the discussion that fills in detail (the conversation), and the tests that record what was agreed (the confirmation). The card is the least important of the three. Good stories pass the INVEST check: independent, negotiable, valuable to users or purchasers, estimatable, small, testable. Write stories for specific kinds of user. Model the user roles first; it stops the team from designing for one imaginary average person. Real users beat stand-ins. When you must use a proxy (a manager, a salesperson, an analyst), know that person's bias and compensate for it. The customer owns priority; the developers own estimates. Neither may do the other's job.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Chapter 1. An Overview In brief: the whole method in miniature: what a story is, where the detail lives, and how stories drive planning and testing. The problem stories solve A software project depends on two groups understanding each other: those who want the product (customers, users, analysts, domain experts) and the technical team. When the business side controls the exchange, scope and dates get dictated with little regard for whether both can be met. When the technical side controls it, jargon takes over and developers stop learning what is needed. Since no project can be predicted in full at the start, the sensible response is to make many small decisions throughout, using a process that surfaces information early and often. Stories are the tool for that. Card, conversation, confirmation A user story describes a piece of functionality that matters to someone who uses or buys the system. It has three aspects, named by Ron Jeffries: Card: one or two sentences, traditionally handwritten on an index card, used for planning and as a reminder. Conversation: the discussions between customer and developers where the details get worked out.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt:
Conversation: the discussions between customer and developers where the details get worked out. Confirmation: the tests that capture those details and show when the story is done. The book quotes Rachel Davies on the role of the card: [Cards] “represent customer requirements rather than document them.” — Rachel Davies, quoted on p. 4 What makes something a story It must be valued by a user or purchaser. A statement about which programming language or database technique to use is not a story for an ordinary business application, because its users do not care. Very large stories are called epics. They are fine as placeholders but must be split before they are built. As a starting guide, a story should take one programmer or one pair somewhere between half a day and about two weeks.

Do not keep splitting just to record every detail. Details belong in the conversation, and the ones that are agreed get noted as short test reminders on the back of the card. Stories are not contracts. Nobody should be able to point at a card months later as proof of what was promised; the tests are the record of agreement.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Why change to stories The chapter previews the case made in Chapter 13: stories favour talking over writing, both sides can read them, they are a convenient unit for planning, they suit iterative work, and they let a team postpone detail until it knows the feature is wanted. Takeaway A story is a promise to have a conversation. The card reminds you to talk; the tests record what you decided. Chapter 2. Writing Stories In brief: six attributes of a good story, remembered by Bill Wake's acronym INVEST, plus how to split and combine stories. Attribute What it means What to do when it fails Independent Stories can be built in any order, so they can be prioritised and estimated separately. Merge the dependent stories into one, or split along a different line. As a last resort write two estimates on the card (done first / done later). Negotiable The card is a reminder, not a specification. Detail is agreed in conversation. Strip excess notes from the front of the card. Keep only the story and open questions; move agreed details to tests on the back. Valuable Someone who uses or pays for the software can see why they want it. Rewrite technology-centred stories in terms of the benefit.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Name the role. One widely used template, from the XP team at Connextra, has three slots: the role, what they want, and the business reason. Write for one user. Singular phrasing exposes ambiguities, such as whether a person may delete only their own records. Use the active voice. The customer writes. Developers may help or suggest, but responsibility stays with the customer, who must understand each story to prioritise it. Do not number the cards. Numbers add overhead and make discussion abstract. Give a card a short title if you need a handle. Remember the purpose. A card is a reminder to talk. Add only enough to pick the conversation up again. My example of slicing (not from the book): for a library app, “A member can reserve a book” is too big. A poor split is “build the reservation screen” and “store reservations”. A better split is “A member can reserve a book that is on the shelf” and “A member can join a waiting list for a book that is out on loan”. Each works end to end. Takeaway Split so that every piece delivers value on its own, name the role, and keep the solution out of the requirement. Part II:

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: When developers wonder exactly what a story means, they note it and keep writing. When discussion drifts into designing a feature, the team stops and writes a story instead. Known specifics go on the card in brackets, and uncertain ones are marked with a question mark. Three cards are constraints: a time limit for a returning customer to find and buy a book, a requirement to share the existing order database, and a concurrent-user capacity. The time limit is framed around the whole task the user performs, not one technical operation, which makes it a better performance requirement. A vague placeholder is acceptable for something not yet thought through, such as reporting. Finding every story is not the goal; finding enough for a preliminary estimate is. Later additions can be swapped in for work of similar size. Chapter 19. Estimating the Stories In brief: the team estimation method from Chapter 8, applied by three programmers with the customer present. Estimating forces clarifying questions. Asking what the customer meant by one search story reveals two modes, so the card is torn up and replaced by two.

Identify what the project's success depends on, and add proxies whose knowledge covers those factors. “While there may not be one customer, there must be one customer voice.” — p. 64 Takeaway A real user is always better than a proxy. If you must use proxies, pick several kinds so their biases offset one another.

Chapter 6. Acceptance Testing User Stories In brief: acceptance tests hold the detail that a story card leaves out, and they define when a story is finished. What the tests are for They record details that came out of customer and developer conversations, in place of long lists of formal requirement statements. They expose assumptions the customer holds but has not said aloud. They give a clear finishing line, which stops the team from doing too little or too much. How testing works with stories Two stages. First jot short test reminders on the back of the card whenever one occurs to someone. Later, turn them into full tests. Before coding. Tests written ahead of programming tell the programmer about cases they might otherwise forget. They are added during conversations, in a focused session at the start of each iteration, and whenever new cases come to light.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt:
Stories support planning and act as prompts for conversation. Origin: use cases are a product of analysis. Stories are an aid to it. Essential use cases (Constantine and Lockwood), stripped of technology assumptions, come close to stories: each user intention could be read as one. Takeaway Think about what users are trying to achieve, not about a list of features the product should have. No amount of up-front thinking fully specifies a non-trivial system.

Chapter 13. Why User Stories? In brief: eight advantages of stories over other techniques, and three honest drawbacks. Advantages They emphasise talking. Written words look precise but are not; a sentence can be parsed two ways, and words such as “should” are open to interpretation. Writing does help memory, but conversation gives a fast feedback loop and no false sense of exactness. Even perfectly worded requirements would not help much: users' views change as they learn, and perfect parts do not guarantee a coherent whole. Everyone can understand them. They are short, free of technical jargon, and always framed by value. Research cited in the book found that people recall events better when they are organised as stories.

turns.question: What is an epic, and when should I split it?
turns.text:
An epic is a story that is too large to estimate or build as it stands. It is useful as a placeholder, but it must be split before anyone builds it [S1][S2].

**When to split**

- **When it's too big to estimate or build.** The INVEST check is the test. If a story fails "Estimatable" or "Small," the fix is usually to split it [S3][S4]. A rough guide is that one programmer or pair should be able to finish a story in about half a day to two weeks [S2].
- **When it won't fit in an iteration.** A small story fits comfortably in one iteration [S4].
- **When it's a compound story.** This is an epic that hides several smaller stories. Split it by operation (create, edit, delete) or by the data involved [S3].
- **When it's a complex story.** This is an epic that is inherently large or uncertain. Split it into a time-boxed spike (an investigation) and a second story for the real work. Where possible, schedule the spike in an earlier iteration [S3].
- **When you're splitting often during planning.** Occasional splitting during iteration planning is normal. If you find yourself doing it frequently, review the remaining stories and split them in advance [S13].

**How to split well**

Make sure each piece delivers value on its own, name the user role, and keep the solution out of the requirement [S7]. Also avoid splitting just to record every detail. Details belong in the conversation with the customer [S2]. Stories that are split too small can also cause problems, because their estimates keep changing. In that case, combine them for planning and split again only when scheduling into an iteration [S14][S15].

sources.excerpt: Constraint A rule the system must obey, such as a performance or capacity target. Recorded on a card but not scheduled like a story. User role A group of users defined by shared characteristics and by how they will use the system. Persona An invented, named individual who represents an important user role. User proxy Someone who stands in for real users on the project. Customer team The people who make sure the product meets users' needs: users, product manager, testers, interaction designers. Acceptance test A test, specified by the customer, that shows a story works as intended. Story point A team-defined, relative unit for the size of a story. Ideal day A working day with no interruptions. A common basis for story points. Velocity Story points completed in an iteration. Only finished stories count. Iteration A fixed period, usually one to four weeks, ending with working, tested software. Release plan A rough allocation of prioritised stories to iterations. Triangulation Checking an estimate by comparing it with stories already estimated. MoSCoW Prioritisation into must have, should have, could have, and won't have this time.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Why break stories into tasks at all Several people often work on one story, by specialism or simply for speed. A story describes value to a user; it is not a to-do list. Listing tasks as a group catches things one person would forget, such as updating the installer or the help text. It is a short burst of just-in-time design, one of many that replace the single up-front design phase of a waterfall project. Guidelines for tasks Separate out any task that is hard to estimate, for instance one that depends on a slow outside decision. Split work that different people could do in parallel. Make a separate task of anything it is useful to know is finished, so others can build on it. There is no required task size. Responsibility is shared A single name goes on each task even when pairing, and that person sees it through. But the commitment is the team's: if someone falls behind, others pick up the work. Nobody gets to say that their part is done while the iteration fails. If a developer finds they have taken on too much, another developer takes some of it, or the customer removes or splits a story. Simply hoping is the third option, and not a good one.

turns.question: How big should a single user story be?
turns.text:
A user story should be small enough to fit comfortably in one iteration, but not so tiny that writing it down costs more than doing it. The library gives no fixed size or point value. [S2]

Other guidance from the study notes:

- **Split anything too big.** If a story is too large to estimate or finish in an iteration, split it. Split epics into smaller stories, and make each piece deliver something usable on its own. [S2][S8]
- **Combine tiny items.** Staple very small work, such as bug fixes or minor UI tweaks, into one story. [S2]
- **Make it estimable.** Developers should be able to make a reasonable guess at its size. If they can't, the gap is missing domain knowledge (ask the customer), missing technical knowledge (run a time-boxed spike), or the story is too big (split it). [S2]
- **Size to the horizon.** Keep stories small and specific for the next few iterations, and broader for later work. [S8]

These points come from the User Stories Applied study notes, which summarise a 2004 book. The library's Scrum Guide and Agile Methods notes don't address story size in the passages I found.

turns.question: Who should write the user stories, and why?
turns.text:
The documents don't name a single author for user stories. They describe a shared job, with the customer or product owner taking the lead and developers helping.

- **The customer (or product owner) writes them.** The User Stories Applied notes assign "writing stories" to the customer, who writes them "in business language, at a suitable size," while developers help by rewording technical needs in terms of user value [S7]. The reason is that stories should describe value the product owner can understand, which makes trading one item for another easier [S9].
- **The Scrum Guide puts the duty on the Product Owner.** The Product Owner is accountable for "creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items" and for ordering them. The Product Owner may delegate this work, but remains accountable for it [S10].
- **Developers help and size the work.** The Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing it, and the Product Owner can help them understand trade-offs [S11][S14].

The main reason for this split is that requirements are a communication problem. The people who want the software and the people who build it see things differently, and stories are meant to prompt conversation rather than act as precise specifications [S4][S3]. The notes also say the customer owns priority and the developers own estimates, and neither should do the other's job [S4].

The sources frame the customer role slightly differently. The User Stories Applied notes speak of the "customer," while the Scrum Guide speaks of the Product Owner. I'm reading these as roughly the same role, but that equivalence is my inference, not something the documents state.

turns.question: What does INVEST stand for?
turns.text:
INVEST is Bill Wake's acronym for six attributes of a good user story: **Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable** [S1][S3].

- **Independent:** stories can be built in any order, so they can be prioritised and estimated separately [S3].
- **Negotiable:** the card is a reminder, not a specification; detail is agreed in conversation [S3].
- **Valuable:** someone who uses or pays for the software can see why they want it [S2][S3].
- **Estimable:** developers can make a reasonable guess at the size [S2].
- **Small:** the story fits comfortably in an iteration [S2].
- **Testable:** there is a way to show it is finished [S2].

turns.question: What is a spike and when should I use one?
turns.text:
A spike is a **time-boxed experiment or investigation** that helps a team learn enough to estimate or plan a story. The library describes it in *User Stories Applied*.

**What it is for:** A story should be estimable, and when developers can't size one, the cause determines the fix. Missing domain knowledge means you ask the customer. Missing technical knowledge means you run a time-boxed experiment, which is a spike [S6][S10].

**When to use one:**
- **The technical approach is unknown.** This is the main case: the team lacks the technical knowledge to estimate the story [S6][S10].
- **A complex story is large or uncertain.** Split it into an investigation with a fixed time limit and a second story for the real work [S1][S9].

**How to plan it:**
- Where you can, schedule the spike in an earlier iteration than the work it informs. This lets the customer prioritise the research separately from the feature, and keeps the iteration from being filled with work nobody can size [S1][S9].

The sources I searched don't go into more detail on spikes, such as their output or how to write their acceptance criteria. The *Agile Methods* study notes and the Scrum Guide didn't surface on this topic in my searches, so I can't say how they treat spikes.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Chapter 1. An Overview In brief: the whole method in miniature: what a story is, where the detail lives, and how stories drive planning and testing. The problem stories solve A software project depends on two groups understanding each other: those who want the product (customers, users, analysts, domain experts) and the technical team. When the business side controls the exchange, scope and dates get dictated with little regard for whether both can be met. When the technical side controls it, jargon takes over and developers stop learning what is needed. Since no project can be predicted in full at the start, the sensible response is to make many small decisions throughout, using a process that surfaces information early and often. Stories are the tool for that. Card, conversation, confirmation A user story describes a piece of functionality that matters to someone who uses or buys the system. It has three aspects, named by Ron Jeffries: Card: one or two sentences, traditionally handwritten on an index card, used for planning and as a reminder. Conversation: the discussions between customer and developers where the details get worked out.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: They are short, free of technical jargon, and always framed by value. Research cited in the book found that people recall events better when they are organised as stories. They are the right size for planning. Formal statements are too many and too tangled to prioritise; use cases and scenarios are too big. They suit iterative development. You can start with an epic and refine it later, and you need not write them all before coding. They encourage deferring detail, so a team under time pressure can start sooner. They support opportunistic development. Studies show that designers do not work strictly top-down; they move between requirements, usage and design as opportunities appear. Stories allow that movement between levels. They encourage participatory design. Because stories are accessible, users become active contributors to deciding how the software behaves. This contrasts with empirical design, in which designers study users but decide alone. They build tacit knowledge. Frequent face-to-face discussion spreads understanding across the team. Drawbacks On a large project with very many stories, it is hard to see how they relate.

turns.question: What's the difference between a compound story and a complex story?
turns.text:
A **compound story** bundles several smaller stories together, while a **complex story** is large or uncertain in itself. The study notes describe both as two kinds of epic, meaning stories too large to estimate or build as they stand [S2].

- **Compound story:** It "hides several smaller stories and can be split, commonly by operation (create, edit, delete) or by the data involved" [S1].
- **Complex story:** It "is inherently large or uncertain." The suggested fix is to "split it into an investigation with a fixed time limit and a second story for the real work" [S1]. That investigation is a spike, which is "a short, time-boxed investigation done to learn enough to estimate or build something" [S2]. Where possible, schedule the spike in an earlier iteration than the work it informs [S1].

In short, you split a compound story into its separate parts, and you split a complex story into a time-boxed investigation followed by the real work. The notes also warn to split along user-facing slices rather than technical layers, so each piece still delivers something usable [S14].

turns.question: How do I make a requirement like "the system must be fast" testable?
turns.text:
The library's main advice is to replace the vague word with a measurable target, stated in a way someone can check.

1. **Replace "fast" with a measurable target.** Give a response time that must be met in a stated percentage of cases [S14]. "Never" and "always" are untestable, so state how often and how fast instead [S13].
2. **Frame the target around the whole task the user performs, not one technical operation.** The book's example is a time limit for a returning customer to find and buy a book, which makes it a better performance requirement [S1].
3. **Ask the right question to find the real need.** Asking "what performance matters, and where?" avoids presuming a speed requirement exists, which "how fast must it be?" does [S3].
4. **Write a concrete test for it.** For performance constraints, the book simulates the stated number of simultaneous users and checks a maximum screen response time [S12]. Include passing and failing cases so the decision is recorded [S12].

An illustrative rewrite (my example, not from the documents): "The system must be fast" becomes "For 95% of returning customers finding and buying a book, the task completes within 3 minutes, with 500 concurrent users." The customer should supply the actual numbers.

turns.question: What are the steps in user role modeling?
turns.text:
Role modeling in *User Stories Applied* has four steps:

1. **Brainstorm.** The customer and developers write role names on cards and place them on a table or wall, saying only the name. No discussion or judging. About fifteen minutes is usually enough. [S1]
2. **Organise.** Move the cards so that overlapping roles physically overlap, by as much as the roles do. [S1]
3. **Consolidate.** Discuss overlapping cards and merge or discard duplicates. Also discard roles that will not affect the product's success. [S1]

turns.question: What is a persona, and when is it worth creating one?
turns.text:
A persona is **an invented, named individual who represents an important user role** [S1]. A user role is a group of users defined by shared characteristics and by how they will use the system [S1].

**When it's worth creating one:**

- **Only for one or two roles.** Personas are an optional extra for "one or two roles that the product must satisfy." For those roles, invent a specific person with a name, a photo and enough background to feel real, then write stories about that person [S2][S10].
- **When it's grounded in real research.** The persona should reflect actual market research [S2][S10].
- **When the roles matter most to success.** The study notes describe asking the customer which roles matter most, then writing personas for those [S3][S9].

**When it may not be worth the effort:**

- The study notes say that for a small project, personas are probably not worth the effort [S3][S9].
- Most teams should stop at the basic role-modeling exercise, which takes about an hour. That exercise means brainstorming role names, consolidating overlaps, and noting attributes such as frequency of use, domain knowledge, computer comfort and goals [S2][S10]. The source says to do this even when real users are nearby [S2][S10].

The study notes' guidance on personas comes from a summary of a 2004 book, so it is a practitioner view rather than a rule from a standard. The documents I have don't cover how to write a persona in detail.

It may reveal stories you would otherwise miss, though there is no easy way to tell whether such stories belong in the product, so spend little time on it. Takeaway Replace “the user” in your stories with a named role. It costs an hour and changes which stories get written. Chapter 4. Gathering Stories In brief: requirements are not lying around waiting to be collected; you go looking for them with several techniques, repeatedly. Trawling, not capturing Words such as “elicit” and “capture” suggest that users already hold every requirement and that, once written down, requirements stay put. The chapter prefers the Robertsons' image of trawling with a net. It fits in four ways: nets of different mesh catch requirements of different sizes, so you can make a coarse first pass and finer ones later; requirements grow in importance or die as the product evolves; you never catch everything, and you catch some rubbish; and skill affects the catch. How much to gather up front Agile teams accept that one pass cannot find everything.

sources.excerpt: Releasing early creates them. Story-writing workshops The fastest way to produce many stories. Hold one before each release. Keep it high level: no screen design, no debating individual stories. One user's remark, quoted in the chapter, sums up why asking “what do you need?” is not enough: “You built exactly what I asked for but it’s not what I want.” — a user, quoted on p. 46 Asking good questions Open-ended: invites more than yes or no. “What would you give up to get X?” reveals tradeoffs that “Would you like X?” hides. Context-free: does not suggest its own answer or presume a requirement exists. Asking how fast a feature must be implies that there is a speed requirement; asking what performance matters, and where, does not. Start broad and move to specific questions later. Take one role or persona at a time. Starting from an empty box for the main screen, ask what that user can do from there; each answer becomes a new box and a story.

turns.question: What techniques can I use to gather user stories?
turns.text:
The User Stories Applied study notes describe four main techniques for gathering stories, plus a few supporting practices.

**The four techniques**
- **User interviews:** the default. Talk to real users across different roles. Users are poor at stating what they need, so they aren't automatically the best people to design the solution. [S9]
- **Questionnaires:** good for getting answers from many users to specific questions, or for prioritising stories you already have. They are one-way and slow, with no follow-up questions, so they are not suitable as the main way to find new stories. [S9]
- **Observation:** watching what people really do, which often differs from what they say they need. Opportunities are rare outside in-house projects, but releasing early creates them. [S9]
- **Story-writing workshops:** the fastest way to produce many stories. Hold one before each release, and keep it high level, with no screen design and no debate over individual stories. [S6, S9]

**Running a workshop**
- Sketch a rough, low-fidelity map of the product (boxes for areas, arrows for how users move between them). It shows workflow, not screens. [S6]
- Take one role or persona at a time, and ask what that user can do from each point. Each answer becomes a new box and a story. [S6, S13]
- Favour quantity over quality. Weak stories can be dropped or given low priority later. [S13]

**Asking good questions**
- Use open-ended questions. "What would you give up to get X?" reveals tradeoffs that "Would you like X?" hides. [S6]
- Keep questions context-free so they don't presume a requirement exists. Ask what performance matters and where, rather than how fast something must be. [S6]
- Start broad and move to specific questions later. [S6]

**Other useful practices**
- **Role modelling first:** identify the distinct kinds of user before writing stories, so you don't design for one imagined user. [S16]
- **User proxies:** when real users are unavailable, a manager, salesperson or analyst can stand in, but each proxy distorts the picture in a predictable way, so check their claims with real users. [S13]
- **Trawling mindset:** the study notes argue that requirements aren't lying around waiting to be collected. You go looking for them with several techniques, repeatedly, and you never catch everything. [S1]
- **Early pass:** look ahead roughly one release (three to six months) and write what you can see, with less detail the further away the work is. [S9]

The study notes stress using several techniques rather than one. [S13]

turns.question: What is an open-ended, context-free question?
turns.text:
An open-ended, context-free question is a way of asking that draws out information without steering the answer.

- **Open-ended:** it "invites more than yes or no." For example, "What would you give up to get X?" reveals tradeoffs that "Would you like X?" hides. [S1]
- **Context-free:** it "does not suggest its own answer or presume a requirement exists." Asking how fast a feature must be is a leading question because it implies a speed requirement. Asking what performance matters, and where, is context-free. [S1]

The study notes recommend starting broad and moving to specific questions later. [S1] They also list asking open-ended, context-free questions as a key skill for finding user stories. [S2]

turns.question: How do I run a story-writing workshop?
turns.text:
The library's main guidance on this comes from the *User Stories Applied* study notes, which describe the workshop as "the fastest way to produce many stories," to be held "before each release" [S1].

**Preparation**
- Identify the user roles or personas first. Stories are written one role at a time, so the roles need to be known in advance [S7].
- Sketch a rough, low-fidelity map of the product on paper or a whiteboard. Boxes are areas of the product and arrows show how users move between them. It shows workflow, not screens [S1].

**Running the session**
1. Take one role or persona at a time. Start from an empty box for the main screen and ask what that user can do from there. Each answer becomes a new box and a story [S1].
2. Ask open-ended, context-free questions. For example, "What would you give up to get X?" reveals tradeoffs that "Would you like X?" hides [S1].
3. Keep it high level. Leave out screen design and don't debate individual stories [S1][S4].
4. If discussion drifts into designing a feature, stop and write a story instead [S7].
5. If developers are unsure what a story means, note it and keep writing. Leave open questions for later [S7].

**Afterwards**
- The workshop yields an initial batch of stories. Developers then estimate them, and the customer prioritises them [S10].
- Expect to split, merge and reword stories as you go [S14].

The 2004 book summarised here is older than the current Scrum Guide. Its workshop advice is about writing stories, and it doesn't cover facilitation details such as timeboxing or room setup, which the library doesn't address. I can search for more on story writing or prioritisation if that helps.

turns.question: Why is a development manager a poor stand-in for real users?
turns.text:
A development manager is a poor stand-in for real users for two main reasons, according to the User Stories Applied study notes:

- **Their interests lean toward the build.** A development manager is "likely to favour interesting technology or a bonus-linked date" [S2].
- **They rarely use the product.** They "rarely ha[ve] hands-on experience as a user" [S2], so they are unlikely to know what ordinary users need.

The notes rank development managers among the worst choices of proxy [S2]. They also say developers are usually worse stand-ins than any of the other proxies listed [S1]. The general rule is that a real user is always better than a proxy. If you must use proxies, pick several kinds so their biases offset one another [S5].

sources.excerpt: Business or systems analyst Often a good proxy, with a foot in both worlds, provided they talk to users instead of reasoning alone, and do not over-invest in up-front analysis. Making the best of a proxy Users exist but access is blocked: ask to set up a user task force of real users as a sounding board. The proxy keeps the final say on direction; day-to-day detail increasingly comes from the task force. No users are reachable: use more than one proxy, of different kinds, so the product is not shaped by one person's needs. Study competing products: reviews and user forums show which features matter and which are too complicated. Release early, even as a beta, to find where the proxy's view and real users' views differ and to open a line to those users. Do not appoint yourself. Developers are usually worse stand-ins than any of the proxies listed. Building the customer team Add real users, ideally one for each important type of user. Name one person as project champion who coordinates the team and makes sure it gives a single, consistent message. Identify what the project's success depends on, and add proxies whose knowledge covers those factors.

turns.question: What can we do if we have no access to real users?
turns.text:
The library's main advice is to use several kinds of proxy, since each one has its own bias. It also says a real user is always better than a proxy.

**What to do**

- **Use more than one proxy, of different kinds,** so the product isn't shaped by one person's needs. Their biases can offset each other. [S1][S6]
- **Pick proxies whose knowledge covers what the project's success depends on.** [S1][S6]
- **Name a project champion** to coordinate the team and give a single, consistent message. "While there may not be one customer, there must be one customer voice." [S1][S6]
- **Study competing products.** Reviews and user forums show which features matter and which are too complicated. [S1]
- **Release early, even as a beta.** This shows where the proxy's view and real users' views differ, and opens a line to real users. [S1]
- **Build personas with care.** For one or two key roles, you can invent a named persona, but it should reflect actual market research. [S5]
- **Don't appoint yourself as the proxy,** and note that developers are usually worse stand-ins than the other proxies. [S1]

**Choosing proxies and their biases**

The sources list typical biases, for example:
- **Users' manager:** may exaggerate problems as they pass up the chain. [S2]
- **Development manager:** may favour interesting technology or a bonus-linked date. [S4]
- **Salesperson:** prioritises whatever feature lost the latest sale. [S4]
- **Domain expert:** may steer the product toward experts like themselves. [S4]
- **Marketing:** tends to value the number of features over their quality. [S4]
- **Customer (the buyer):** may never use the product. [S4]
- **Business or systems analyst:** often a good proxy, provided they talk to users rather than reasoning alone. [S4]

Whichever proxy you use, check their claims with real users where you can. [S2][S4]

**If users exist but access is blocked**

Ask to set up a user task force of real users as a sounding board. The proxy keeps the final say on direction, while day-to-day detail increasingly comes from the task force. [S1]

These points come from *User Stories Applied* study notes, which summarise a 2004 book, so they are not Scrum Guide rules.

Consolidate. Discuss overlapping cards; merge or tear up duplicates. Also discard roles that will not affect the product's success. Refine. Add distinguishing attributes to each remaining card.

Useful attributes to note for each role: how often they will use the software, how well they know the domain, their general comfort with computers, their skill with this particular product, and what they mainly want from it (speed, convenience, a rich experience, and so on). Guidance A role should stand for one person, not an organisation. A company cannot use software; a recruiter at that company can. Keep roles human where possible. Add another system as a role only if it helps the team think. The whole exercise should take about an hour, and most teams should stop there. Do it even when real users sit nearby. Available users are not necessarily the right mix of users. Two optional extras Personas. For one or two roles that the product must satisfy, invent a specific person with a name, a photo and enough background to feel real, and write stories about that person. Make sure the persona reflects actual market research. Extreme characters.

turns.question: Who writes the acceptance tests, and when?
turns.text:
The customer writes the acceptance tests, usually with help from programmers. Testing is part of development, and the customer specifies the tests "because the software exists to realise the customer's vision." Developers may add tests of their own [S7]. The book's project has no dedicated tester, so programmers help the customer write them [S1].

Timing:
- **Early, before coding:** Tests written ahead of programming tell the programmer about cases they might otherwise forget [S2].
- **Start of each iteration:** They are added in a focused session at the start of each iteration, and whenever new cases come to light [S2].
- **Two stages:** Short test reminders are jotted on the story card first, then turned into full tests later [S2].
- **Every iteration:** The customer should run the acceptance tests at least at the end of each iteration, including earlier tests, because new work can break old work [S7].

The tests also serve as the record of what was agreed, since stories themselves are not contracts [S8].

The documents I have don't say who writes acceptance tests in Scrum specifically. The Scrum Guide excerpts I found cover the sprint review and increment, not test ownership.

sources.excerpt: Chapter 21. The Acceptance Tests In brief: the customer writes tests for each planned story, helped by the programmers because the project has no dedicated tester. Writing tests prompts more conversation and exposes unanswered questions, for example what happens with items that are out of stock. It can simplify the product. The team realises that a “remove from cart” story is a special case of changing a quantity, and replaces it with one more general story. Tests record decisions, such as which payment cards are accepted, by including both passing and failing cases. Tests cover permissions (what a non-administrator must not be able to do) and side effects (what happens to open orders when a book is deleted or repriced). Each constraint gets a concrete test: checking that an order placed online appears in the shared database, and simulating the stated number of simultaneous users with a maximum screen response time. The customer owns priority; the developers own estimates. Neither may do the other's job. Estimate in relative units (story points) as a team, then let measured velocity turn points into calendar time. Plan at two levels. A release plan is a rough allocation of stories to iterations. An iteration plan breaks the next few stories into tasks that individuals sign up for.

Distant work stays as large placeholder stories; near work is split small. Expect the plan to change and re-plan every iteration. Part I: Getting Started The first seven chapters cover what a story is, how to write one, who it is for, how to find stories, who can speak for users, how stories are tested, and a set of writing guidelines. Chapter 1. An Overview In brief: the whole method in miniature: what a story is, where the detail lives, and how stories drive planning and testing.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: A list of attributes can describe the wrong product entirely. The book's illustration: a list specifying an engine, four wheels and a steering wheel suggests a car, while the user's actual goals (cut the grass quickly and comfortably) call for a ride-on mower. The customer cannot see the cost of each item while writing the wish list. With stories, each one carries an estimate from the start. A document passed back and forth between departments, each rewriting it under a new name, is a sign that people are preparing to assign blame. Stories and use cases Scope: stories are deliberately kept small enough to schedule. Completeness: a story together with its acceptance tests carries about the same information as a use case; the tests correspond to the use case's extensions. Longevity: use cases are permanent artefacts. Stories are not meant to outlive the iteration that implements them. Purpose: use cases document agreement between customer and developers. Stories support planning and act as prompts for conversation. Origin: use cases are a product of analysis. Stories are an aid to it.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: They are added during conversations, in a focused session at the start of each iteration, and whenever new cases come to light. The customer specifies them, with help from testers and programmers, because the software exists to realise the customer's vision. Developers may add tests of their own. Testing is part of development, not a phase after it. A tester who learns the system only from programmers ends up checking that the code does what the programmer said, not what users want. Know when to stop. Write tests while they add clarity. The customer need not cover every lowlevel case; programmers' unit tests should do that. Prompts that help the customer find tests: is there anything further the programmers should be told, which of my assumptions about the implementation are unstated, in what circumstances would the behaviour differ, and what could fail? Automation The customer should run the acceptance tests at least at the end of every iteration, including those from earlier iterations, since new work can break old work. That grows expensive, so automate where possible.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Stories are not contracts. Nobody should be able to point at a card months later as proof of what was promised; the tests are the record of agreement. How a story-driven project runs A customer team (product manager, real users, testers, interaction designers) writes the stories, because stories must be in business language and the customer has to prioritise them. An initial batch usually comes out of a story-writing workshop. Developers estimate each story. Customer and developers pick an iteration length, typically one to four weeks, and keep it fixed. Developers guess their velocity: how much estimated work fits in one iteration. The first guess will be wrong and gets replaced by measurement. A release plan is made by filling iterations in priority order without exceeding velocity. Each iteration delivers working code for its stories; the customer specifies tests during the iteration and adjusts the plan before the next one. If the next story in priority order does not fit in what remains of an iteration, there are two options: pull forward a smaller, lower-priority story, or split the large story and take its most important part.

turns.question: What does "slice the cake" mean when splitting a story?
turns.text:
"Slice the cake" means splitting a story so that each piece runs through every layer of the system and delivers something usable on its own. Avoid splits along technical lines, such as "the form" and "the database write", because those pieces are useless alone [S3].

The source gives a library example. "A member can reserve a book" is too big. Splitting it into "build the reservation screen" and "store reservations" is a poor split. A better split is "A member can reserve a book that is on the shelf" and "A member can join a waiting list for a book that is out on loan". Each works end to end [S2]. The source notes this example is the author's own, not from the book [S2].

sources.excerpt: Combine them for planning; split again only when scheduling into an iteration. Interdependent stories Iterations are hard to plan because stories drag other stories in with them. Increase visibility: brief daily meetings, end-of-iteration demonstrations, and QA involvement in story conversations. Too many details More time goes on writing about stories than discussing them. Rely on conversation. Tom Poppendieck's advice, quoted below, is to shrink the card. UI detail too soon Early stories mention particular screens or controls. Rewrite to describe what the user does, without assuming a layout. Thinking too far ahead Cards overflow; someone proposes a detailed template or finer-grained estimates. Recall why the team chose stories: requirements cannot all be known in advance. Splitting too many stories Stories are routinely split during iteration planning to make things fit. Occasional splitting is normal. If frequent, review the remaining stories and split in advance.

sources.excerpt: Why break stories into tasks at all Several people often work on one story, by specialism or simply for speed. A story describes value to a user; it is not a to-do list. Listing tasks as a group catches things one person would forget, such as updating the installer or the help text. It is a short burst of just-in-time design, one of many that replace the single up-front design phase of a waterfall project. Guidelines for tasks Separate out any task that is hard to estimate, for instance one that depends on a slow outside decision. Split work that different people could do in parallel. Make a separate task of anything it is useful to know is finished, so others can build on it. There is no required task size. Responsibility is shared A single name goes on each task even when pairing, and that person sees it through. But the commitment is the team's: if someone falls behind, others pick up the work. Nobody gets to say that their part is done while the iteration fails. If a developer finds they have taken on too much, another developer takes some of it, or the customer removes or splits a story. A statement about which programming language or database technique to use is not a story for an ordinary business application, because its users do not care. Very large stories are called epics. They are fine as placeholders but must be split before they are built. As a starting guide, a story should take one programmer or one pair somewhere between half a day and about two weeks.

Do not keep splitting just to record every detail. Details belong in the conversation, and the ones that are agreed get noted as short test reminders on the back of the card. Valuable Someone who uses or pays for the software can see why they want it. Rewrite technology-centred stories in terms of the benefit. Best fix: let the customer write the stories. Estimatable Developers can make a reasonable guess at size. Missing domain knowledge: ask the customer. Missing technical knowledge: run a time-boxed experiment (a spike). Too big: split it.

Small Fits comfortably in an iteration, yet is not so tiny that writing it down costs more than doing it. Split epics; staple tiny items (bug fixes, small UI tweaks) together into one story. turns.question: How should nonfunctional requirements like performance be handled?
turns.text:
Nonfunctional requirements such as performance are usually handled as **constraints**, not as ordinary stories.

- **Write them on a constraint card.** The book recommends writing nonfunctional needs (performance, availability, security, capacity and others) on a card marked as a constraint, and where practical checking them with an automated test that runs at least daily [S4]. Rules the system must obey, such as capacity, platforms or uptime, are not scheduled like stories but should be backed by an automated test where possible [S8].
- **Frame performance around the user's task.** A good performance constraint describes the whole task the user performs, not one technical operation. The book's example is a time limit for a returning customer to find and buy a book [S1].
- **Elicit it with open questions.** Ask what performance matters and where, rather than asking how fast a feature must be, because the second question assumes a speed requirement exists [S7].
- **Plan the testing.** Story tests are mostly functional. Depending on the product, the book also suggests planning for performance and stress testing [S6].
- **Keep the solution out.** Stating a solution inside a requirement closes off design options, so keep the user interface out of the requirement for as long as you can [S8].

These points come from the User Stories Applied study notes, which summarise Mike Cohn's 2004 book. The library's other documents don't cover nonfunctional requirements in detail.

turns.question: What is a story point?
turns.text:
A story point is a **relative unit for sizing a user story**. Each team defines its own unit. It can be an ideal day, an ideal week, or a measure of complexity [S1]. An ideal day is a working day with no meetings or interruptions, and Cohn prefers it as the basis because it is easier to think in than elapsed time and easier to convert to a schedule later [S1][S3].

Key points from the library:

- **Estimated by the team.** Story estimates belong to the whole team, not one person [S3].
- **Used with velocity.** Velocity is the number of points a team completes in an iteration. Measured velocity then turns points into calendar time [S5][S7].
- **Relative, not comparable across teams.** Points are not comparable between teams [S2].
- **Kept consistent.** Teams compare new estimates with stories already sized (triangulation). A four-point story should look about twice a two-point one [S2]. Many teams use a fixed scale such as ½, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 80 [S2].

The library's source is the User Stories Applied study notes, which summarise Mike Cohn's 2004 book. The Scrum Guide (2020) in the library doesn't cover story points, so this answer comes from the study notes alone.

turns.question: How does the team estimation process work, step by step?
turns.text:
The team estimation method in the library comes from Mike Cohn's approach as summarised in *User Stories Applied*. It works like this:

1. **Read the story.** The customer reads out the story and answers the developers' questions. [S10]
2. **Estimate privately.** Each developer privately writes an estimate on a card. [S10]
3. **Reveal together.** Everyone shows their cards at once. [S10]
4. **Explain the extremes.** The highest and lowest estimators explain their reasoning. The aim is to learn what they were thinking, not to challenge them. [S10]
5. **Estimate again.** After a short discussion, everyone estimates again. [S10]
6. **Repeat until close.** Repeat until the numbers are close. It seldom takes more than three rounds. [S10]
7. **Settle on a figure.** Exact agreement is not required, only a reasonable figure. [S10]

A few related points from the same notes:

- **Estimates belong to the whole team,** because nobody yet knows who will do the work and group estimates are more reliable. [S10]
- **The customer attends but does not estimate** and does not react to the numbers. [S10]
- **Estimates should cover everything needed to finish the story,** including testing and time spent with the customer. [S10]
- **Check consistency by triangulating.** Compare each new estimate with stories already sized. A four-point story should look about twice a two-point one. [S10]
- **Use story points.** Each team defines its unit, such as an ideal day, an ideal week, or a complexity measure. [S1]
- **Expect clarifying questions.** Estimating often reveals ambiguity. In one example, a vague search story was split into two cards. [S3]

The notes present this as the method used in a sample project, where three programmers estimated with the customer present. [S8] The notes also say a team's velocity is what turns these points into calendar time. [S6]

sources.excerpt: Stories are not contracts. Nobody should be able to point at a card months later as proof of what was promised; the tests are the record of agreement. How a story-driven project runs A customer team (product manager, real users, testers, interaction designers) writes the stories, because stories must be in business language and the customer has to prioritise them. An initial batch usually comes out of a story-writing workshop. Developers estimate each story. Customer and developers pick an iteration length, typically one to four weeks, and keep it fixed. Developers guess their velocity: how much estimated work fits in one iteration. The first guess will be wrong and gets replaced by measurement. A release plan is made by filling iterations in priority order without exceeding velocity. Each iteration delivers working code for its stories; the customer specifies tests during the iteration and adjusts the plan before the next one. If the next story in priority order does not fit in what remains of an iteration, there are two options: pull forward a smaller, lower-priority story, or split the large story and take its most important part.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: They are short, free of technical jargon, and always framed by value. Research cited in the book found that people recall events better when they are organised as stories. They are the right size for planning. Formal statements are too many and too tangled to prioritise; use cases and scenarios are too big. They suit iterative development. You can start with an epic and refine it later, and you need not write them all before coding. They encourage deferring detail, so a team under time pressure can start sooner. They support opportunistic development. Studies show that designers do not work strictly top-down; they move between requirements, usage and design as opportunities appear. Stories allow that movement between levels. They encourage participatory design. Because stories are accessible, users become active contributors to deciding how the software behaves. This contrasts with empirical design, in which designers study users but decide alone. They build tacit knowledge. Frequent face-to-face discussion spreads understanding across the team. Drawbacks On a large project with very many stories, it is hard to see how they relate.

turns.question: How do we estimate velocity for a brand-new team?
turns.text:
For a brand-new team with no history, the library suggests three ways to get a first velocity figure:

1. **Use the team's history**, if the same team has just finished similar work. [S2]
2. **Run one iteration and measure.** [S2]
3. **Make a reasoned guess.** If a point is an ideal day, a common starting assumption is that velocity will be between a third and a half of the developer-days in an iteration. [S2]

**Worked examples from the library:**
- Four developers on two-week iterations give 40 developer-days, so a starting velocity of about 13 to 20 points is plausible. [S2]
- Two programmers over ten working days is twenty programmer-days. Assuming two to three real days per ideal day gives a range of seven to ten points, and the team cautiously picked eight. [S7]

**Using the guess:**
- Divide the total points by velocity to estimate the number of iterations. A 120-point release at 13 to 20 points per iteration would take roughly six to nine iterations. [S2]
- Don't commit to dates from this. A release plan supports statements like "about five to seven iterations", not a specific calendar date. [S2]
- Early velocity is volatile, so don't draw conclusions from one or two iterations. [S3]
- Plan for a checkpoint. With two-week iterations, the team gets one chance to measure velocity and adjust before the plan is final. [S7] If the first iteration goes better or worse than expected, stories can be moved between iterations by agreement with the customer. [S7]

**Making the measurement reliable:**
- Count only stories that pass their acceptance tests. Partly finished stories count for nothing. [S4]
- Use the points assigned before the iteration. Don't rescore a story because it turned out harder; apply that learning to future estimates. [S3]

Note that these velocity methods come from the *User Stories Applied* study notes, which summarise a 2004 book. The library's Scrum Guide passages don't address how to estimate velocity.

turns.question: What are the MoSCoW rules?
turns.text:
MoSCoW is a prioritisation scheme from DSDM with four categories:

- **Must have:** required.
- **Should have:** important, but a short-term workaround exists. [S1]
- **Could have:** dropped if time runs out. [S1]
- **Won't have this time:** explicitly out of the current scope. [S2, S3]

The study notes also make a few practical points:

- The end result should be a specific order (first, second, third), not just groups. [S1]
- Developers contribute technical factors, such as the risk that a story cannot be done as hoped and the effect on other stories of postponing it. The customer weighs how many users want a story, how much a few important users want it, and whether it belongs with other stories. [S1]
- If a story is hard to rank, it probably mixes parts of different importance, so split it. [S1]
- In one worked example, the customer sorted cards into the four piles while considering cost as well as value. [S5]

The MoSCoW rules from DSDM are a useful alternative: must have, should have (important, but a short-term workaround exists), could have (dropped if time runs out), won't have this time. The customer needs the estimates to prioritise, because cost changes desirability. If a story is hard to rank, it probably mixes parts of different importance. Development manager Among the worst choices: likely to favour interesting technology or a bonuslinked date, and rarely has hands-on experience as a user. turns.question: Who has the final say on priorities, the developers or the customer?
turns.text:
The Product Owner has the final say on priorities. Neither the developers nor the customer as a group decides.

- **Product Owner:** The Scrum Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for ordering Product Backlog items, and the Product Owner "is one person, not a committee." turns.question: What happens in an iteration planning meeting?
turns.text:
An iteration planning meeting is the start-of-iteration meeting where the team decides what it will build next. The library's sources describe it in two ways: *User Stories Applied* describes the meeting step by step, and the Scrum Guide describes the equivalent event, Sprint Planning.

**Step by step (User Stories Applied)**
- **Discuss a story.** The customer reads the top-priority story. Developers ask enough questions to break it down, though finer points are settled during the iteration. The customer can also announce changed priorities here. [S2]
- **Break it into tasks.** Tasks are written up as people call them out, because several people often work on one story. [S2]
- **Accept responsibility.** One developer puts their name against each task. [S2]
- **Repeat** for further stories until the work discussed matches the team's velocity. [S2]
- **Estimate and confirm.** Each developer estimates their own tasks in ideal time and judges whether the total is achievable. [S2]

The goal is to say who does what in the coming weeks and test whether it fits. [S1] The customer should hold new ideas until the next planning meeting rather than change priorities mid-iteration. [S1]

**Sprint Planning (Scrum Guide 2020)**
Sprint Planning answers three questions: [S12]
1. **Why is this Sprint valuable?** The Product Owner proposes how the product could grow in value, and the whole Scrum Team agrees a Sprint Goal. The Sprint Goal must be finalised before planning ends. [S9]
2. **What can be done this Sprint?** Developers select Product Backlog items through discussion with the Product Owner, using knowledge of past performance, upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done. [S9]
3. **How will the work get done?** Developers plan the work for each selected item, often breaking it into pieces of a day or less. [S9]

The Sprint Goal, the selected items and the delivery plan together form the Sprint Backlog. [S9] Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and is usually shorter for shorter Sprints. [S8]

The two sources differ slightly in emphasis. The Scrum Guide adds the Sprint Goal and the Product Owner's role in framing value, which the user-stories description does not cover. The *User Stories Applied* notes are a 2004 summary and do not mention a Sprint Goal. Where the sources differ, the Scrum Guide is the authoritative definition of Scrum.

turns.question: Do partially finished stories count toward velocity?
turns.text:
No. Partly finished stories count for zero. Velocity is the points of stories that pass their acceptance tests, and half-done stories count as zero [S3]. The rule is that a story counts only when it is completely finished, meaning it passes its acceptance tests [S2].

The reasons given are that estimating a percentage complete is unreliable, incomplete work has no value to users, and the last tenth of a story can hide a lot of difficulty [S1].

The source suggests two things to do about stories that regularly end an iteration half-done:
- If partial stories often change the velocity, the stories are probably too big [S1].
- If many stories end the iteration half-done, the team is not working together. It is better to finish some stories and leave the others unstarted [S1].

If a story turns out harder than expected, don't rescore it after the iteration. Use what you learned to adjust estimates for future stories [S1].

These points come from the User Stories Applied study notes, which summarise Mike Cohn's 2004 book. My searches did not return anything on velocity from the 2020 Scrum Guide.

turns.question: What's the difference between an iteration burndown chart and a daily burndown chart?
turns.text:
The main difference is the unit and the purpose. An **iteration burndown** tracks points at the release level, while a **daily burndown** tracks hours within the current iteration.

- **Iteration burndown:** Shows the points remaining at the end of each iteration, including work added or re-estimated. It shows net progress toward the release, and the line can rise if scope grows faster than work is completed [S3].
- **Daily burndown:** Shows the estimated hours of task work remaining on each day of the current iteration. It is used to manage the iteration in progress [S1].

The two charts also differ in how the team uses them. Teams should track hours remaining, not hours spent, and developers can update their own remaining estimates on a shared board at the end of each day or when a task ends [S1].

The Agile Methods notes describe the Sprint Burndown Chart in the same daily way, showing the work remaining in a sprint day by day to help predict whether the sprint goal will be met on time [S2]. Those notes also say the Scrum Guide treats the burndown chart as an optional forecasting practice rather than a required artifact [S4]. Burn-down charts can help forecast progress, but they do not replace empiricism [S14].

turns.question: How are user stories different from use cases?
turns.text:
Use cases and user stories both describe what users need, but they differ in size, purpose, and lifespan. The main points, from the *User Stories Applied* study notes, are:

- **Size:** A story is much finer-grained than a use case. A story is roughly one path through a use case, and one scenario may span several use cases [S1]. Stories are kept small enough to schedule [S4].
- **Purpose:** Use cases document an agreement between customer and developers. Stories support planning and act as prompts for conversation [S4].
- **Origin:** Use cases are a product of analysis. Stories are an aid to it [S3, S4].
- **Lifespan:** Use cases are permanent artefacts. Stories are not meant to outlive the iteration that implements them [S4].
- **Focus:** A story expresses a user's goal, while a list of attributes describes a solution [S1]. Use cases have a main success path plus extensions [S2].
- **Completeness:** A story plus its acceptance tests carries about the same information as a use case, and the tests correspond to the use case's extensions [S4].

The notes also say that use cases have a built-in hierarchy that stories lack, so on large projects it can be harder to see how stories relate [S15].

These comparisons come from the study notes' summary of Mike Cohn's 2004 book. The notes don't say whether the book's view is the only one in the field.

turns.question: What are the drawbacks of user stories?
turns.text:
The study notes name three drawbacks of user stories, with a related tradeoff:

- **Hard to see how stories relate on large projects.** With very many stories, it is hard to see how they connect. Using roles and keeping stories at a higher level until needed helps. Use cases have a built-in hierarchy that stories lack. [S2][S3]
- **Extra documentation for traceability.** If the process requires traceability from requirements to tests, extra documentation is needed, though it can be kept light. [S2]
- **Conversation does not scale to very large teams.** Some things must be written down. [S2]

The notes also describe a tradeoff: many people knowing a little from documents versus fewer people knowing a lot from discussion. [S2]

These points come from the User Stories Applied study notes, which summarise Mike Cohn's 2004 book. The Scrum Guide does not address them.

turns.question: What is goldplating and how do we prevent it?
turns.text:
**Goldplating** is when developers add features nobody asked for, or interpret a story more generously than it was written. [S14] [S1]

The library suggests these ways to prevent it:

- **Increase visibility.** Use brief daily meetings, end-of-iteration demonstrations, and QA involvement in story conversations. [S1]
- **Check each piece of work against its goal.** The Agile Methods notes suggest asking of any Scrum work which goal it serves and whether it meets the Definition of Done. If it is not Done, it is not part of the Increment. [S6]
- **Use the Definition of Done as a gate.** The Scrum Guide says work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done, and an item that does not meet it cannot be presented at the Sprint Review. [S3] [S7] The documents don't explicitly link this rule to goldplating, so treat it as a related control rather than a direct fix.
- **Keep stories focused on user value.** The User Stories notes advise rewriting stories to describe what the user does, not a particular screen or layout, and relying on conversation to create shared understanding rather than heavy documentation. [S1] [S13]

turns.question: Should we write stories on paper cards or in software?
turns.text:
The library's answer is to start with cards and switch to software only when you have a clear reason. Mike Cohn's advice is "start with cards, and switch only when there is a strong reason." [S2]

**Paper cards suit you when:**
- The team sits together. Cards are easy to sort, stack, pin up and carry to meetings, and they encourage discussion. [S2]
- You want to keep stories short. Limited space on a card keeps them brief. [S2]
- You want to be reminded that stories are imprecise. [S2]

**Software suits you when:**
- The team or customer is not in one place. [S2]
- You need formal traceability, for example for ISO certification. [S2]
- You need more room for acceptance tests than the back of a card gives. [S2]
- You need stories that don't get lost and that remote stakeholders can see. [S2]

Whichever you choose, the card is the least important part of a story. The conversation fills in the detail, and the tests record what was agreed. [S4] Cohn also recommends keeping finished stories rather than tearing up the cards, because archived stories have been useful later. [S3]

These points come from the User Stories Applied study notes, which summarise a 2004 book. The documents I have don't say which tool suits a particular team beyond this.

turns.question: List all 27 stories from the example project.
turns.text:
I can't list the 27 individual stories. The library confirms the number but not their text.

The example is the mail-order sailing supplies seller's online book store in Part IV of the User Stories Applied study notes. The Chapter 18 workshop "yields 27 cards, covering search, book details, a shopping cart, checkout, ratings and reviews, accounts, wish lists, order history, recommendations, gift options, reports and administration" [S19]. The notes don't give the card wording, so I can't list them.

The notes do describe some of the related work:
- **Roles:** Eight user roles remain after consolidation, including four kinds of sailor, a gift buyer, a librarian, an administrator and a viewer of management reports [S19].
- **Constraints:** Three cards are constraints: a time limit for a returning customer to find and buy a book, a requirement to share the existing order database, and a concurrent-user capacity [S23].
- **Acceptance tests:** Chapter 21 gives examples such as permission tests and side-effect tests, for instance what happens to open orders when a book is deleted or repriced [S15].

The full card list would be in the book itself, which isn't in this library.

The ideas are the author’s; the wording is not. Short quotations are marked and attributed. About these notes These are study notes on User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development by Mike Cohn (Addison-Wesley, 2004). They follow the book's own order: five parts, twenty-one chapters and an appendix on Extreme Programming. Everything here is a summary in my own words, written to help a reader recall and apply the ideas. It is not a substitute for the book, which contains the full arguments, the worked examples, the figures, and end-of-chapter questions with answers. A handful of short quotations are marked and given a page number from the printed edition. Where an example is not the book's own, it is labelled as mine. Each chapter section has the same shape: a one-line summary, the main ideas, and a takeaway. A glossary and two quick-reference tables are at the end.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: A detailed narrative of particular people using the product in a setting, with goals, actions and events. Size next to a story Much finer grained; many statements per story. Usually larger. A story is roughly one path through a use case. Larger still. One scenario may span several use cases. Main contrast Lists attributes of a solution, where a story expresses a user's goal. Cost is not visible until everything is written. Written to record an agreement and kept for the life of the product. Prone to UI detail. Far more detail, and detail of a different kind. Against the big specification Such documents are slow to write, error-prone and tedious to read, so people skim them and miss the overall picture. They cannot be completed up front, because users change their minds once they see working software. Calling that a “change of scope” wrongly implies the scope was ever fully known, and that software is finished when it meets a list, not when it meets users' goals. A list of attributes can describe the wrong product entirely.

sources.excerpt: Colour-coding cards by type is, in his view, more trouble than it is worth. Takeaway Match the tool to the project. Use constraints for system-wide qualities, and give the interface early attention when it is central to the product. Part IV: An Example Chapters 17 to 21 follow one small invented project from first meeting to acceptance tests. A longestablished mail-order seller of sailing supplies wants to start selling online, beginning with books only, and wants the site live in thirty days. A vice president of sales and marketing, Lori, acts as customer. The example is useful mainly for seeing the techniques used in sequence, so the notes below record what each chapter demonstrates. Chapter 17. The User Roles In brief: the role-modeling steps from Chapter 3, applied. Because the real buyers are outside the company, an internal person must act as proxy customer. The team brainstorms a dozen role cards, lays them out by overlap, and consolidates. Nearduplicates are merged, a role naming an organisation is replaced by one naming a person, and a role tied to a job title is renamed more generically.

sources.title: User Stories Applied: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: Why break stories into tasks at all Several people often work on one story, by specialism or simply for speed. A story describes value to a user; it is not a to-do list. Listing tasks as a group catches things one person would forget, such as updating the installer or the help text. It is a short burst of just-in-time design, one of many that replace the single up-front design phase of a waterfall project. Guidelines for tasks Separate out any task that is hard to estimate, for instance one that depends on a slow outside decision. Split work that different people could do in parallel. Make a separate task of anything it is useful to know is finished, so others can build on it. There is no required task size. Responsibility is shared A single name goes on each task even when pairing, and that person sees it through. But the commitment is the team's: if someone falls behind, others pick up the work. Nobody gets to say that their part is done while the iteration fails. If a developer finds they have taken on too much, another developer takes some of it, or the customer removes or splits a story. Simply hoping is the third option, and not a good one.

That grows expensive, so automate where possible. The book recommends Ward Cunningham's Framework for Integrated Test (FIT) and FitNesse, which builds on it: the customer writes inputs and expected results as rows in a table, a programmer writes the small amount of glue code, and results show as green or red cells. Other kinds of testing Story tests are mostly functional. Depending on the product, also plan for user-interface testing, usability testing, performance testing and stress testing. The aim on an agile project is to find and remove defects using judgement and experience, without chasing complete coverage and without blame when something slips through. Takeaway Tests are how stories carry detail. Write them early, have the customer own them, and automate them so they can run every iteration.

Chapter 7. Guidelines for Good Stories In brief: thirteen practical habits for writing better stories. Start from goals. For each role, list what that user is trying to achieve with the product; those goals are high-level stories that lead to others. Slice the cake. When splitting, make each piece run through every layer of the system so it delivers something usable.

sources.excerpt: A list of attributes can describe the wrong product entirely. The book's illustration: a list specifying an engine, four wheels and a steering wheel suggests a car, while the user's actual goals (cut the grass quickly and comfortably) call for a ride-on mower. The customer cannot see the cost of each item while writing the wish list. With stories, each one carries an estimate from the start. A document passed back and forth between departments, each rewriting it under a new name, is a sign that people are preparing to assign blame. Stories and use cases Scope: stories are deliberately kept small enough to schedule. Completeness: a story together with its acceptance tests carries about the same information as a use case; the tests correspond to the use case's extensions. Longevity: use cases are permanent artefacts. Stories are not meant to outlive the iteration that implements them. Purpose: use cases document agreement between customer and developers. Stories support planning and act as prompts for conversation. Origin: use cases are a product of analysis. Stories are an aid to it.

Chapter 13. Why User Stories? In brief: eight advantages of stories over other techniques, and three honest drawbacks. Advantages They emphasise talking. Written words look precise but are not; a sentence can be parsed two ways, and words such as “should” are open to interpretation.
